lead: An optical source emits light into a wide cone, but a fiber accepts only a narrow cone and a small core area. Source-to-fiber coupling gets the most light from the source into the guided mode. Coupling efficiency η is the ratio of coupled power to emitted power. It depends on source radiance, fiber numerical aperture (NA), core area and alignment. Only a few universities teach the full calculation. The same ideas set transmitter design, pigtailing and package tolerances.
prereq: You need: 3.2 LED emission and numerical aperture and acceptance angle from fiber basics.

blocks.text: Direct coupling puts the fiber face close to the source with no lens. The source emits over area A<sub>s</sub> and into a cone. The fiber accepts only rays inside its acceptance cone and over its core area A<sub>c</sub>. Rays outside either limit are lost.
Radiance L is power per area per solid angle, in W m⁻² sr⁻¹. A high-L source packs more power into the small cone and spot a fiber accepts.

blocks.where: η is coupling efficiency (0 to 1); P<sub>f</sub> is power in the guided mode (W); P<sub>s</sub> is power emitted by the source (W).
NA = sin θ<sub>a</sub> is the fiber numerical aperture; θ<sub>a</sub> is the acceptance angle in air; the source area is no larger than the core and fills a hemisphere.

blocks.text: For a Lambertian source the fraction of emitted power inside the acceptance cone is sin²θ<sub>a</sub> = NA², so NA enters squared. The small-angle approximation of the accepted solid angle gives the same number. A laser's narrow beam can beat this LED estimate.

In terms of the source radiance B0 (W cm⁻² sr⁻¹) and emitting radius rs, a Lambertian surface emits Ps = π²rs²B0 in all. A step-index fiber of core radius a takes P = π²rs²B0NA² when rs ≤ a, and P = π²a²B0NA² when rs > a. Dividing by Ps gives the two efficiency formulas of this chapter.
Fresnel reflection at an uncoated air-glass face (n ≈ 1.5) removes near 4% of the light, R = ((n − 1)/(n + 1))² ≈ 0.04, even with perfect alignment. In dB that is −10 log₁₀(1 − R) ≈ 0.18 dB per face.

sections.h3: Large source area and coupling improvement

blocks.text: When the source area is larger than the core, only the part of the source that images onto the core can couple. For uniform emission, add the area ratio:

blocks.where: r<sub>c</sub> is core radius (m); r<sub>s</sub> is source emitting radius (m); NA is numerical aperture. Use radii in the same unit. The area factor is a power ratio, not an amplitude ratio.

blocks.text: A lens can match the source image to the core, but shrinking the image widens the ray angles at the fiber face, so for a large Lambertian source a lens cannot raise η above the (r<sub>c</sub>/r<sub>s</sub>)² NA² limit. A lens helps most with a small source: it spreads the image to fill the core and reduces ray angles, pushing η above NA². A tapered or lensed fiber does the same gradually. Pigtailing fixes the fiber to the source in one package; index-matching glue or an anti-reflection coating cuts Fresnel loss.

Alignment tolerance follows spot size. A single-mode core is near 9 µm, so lateral error must be under about 1 µm. A 50 µm multimode core is looser. Coupling loss is quoted in dB; 3 dB means half the power is lost.

figure.caption: The worked example to scale: a Lambertian LED face of radius 100 µm butted against a 50 µm-radius core with NA 0.20. Only the central quarter of the face lies over the core, and only rays inside the 11.5° acceptance cone are guided, so 1% of the 2.0 mW, 20 µW, is launched.

examples.question: A Lambertian LED has emitting-area radius 100 µm. A step-index fiber has core radius 50 µm and NA = 0.20. Total LED power is 2.0 mW. The source area is larger and uniform. Find the coupled power.
steps: Both radii are in µm: r<sub>s</sub> = 100 µm, r<sub>c</sub> = 50 µm.
P<sub>f</sub> = η P<sub>s</sub> = 0.01 × 2.0 mW = 0.02 mW = 20 µW.
examples.answer: The coupled power is 20 µW, with coupling efficiency 0.01.
examples.check:
r_s = 100e-6
r_c = 50e-6
NA = 0.20
P_s = 2.0e-3
eta = (r_c/r_s)**2 * NA**2
P_f = eta * P_s
print(f"{eta:.4f}")
print(f"{P_f*1e3:.4f}")
print(f"{P_f*1e6:.1f}")

examples.question: A surface-emitting LED has radiance B<sub>0</sub> = 100 W cm⁻² sr⁻¹ and emitting radius 35 µm. It is butted against a step-index fiber with core radius 25 µm, NA = 0.20 and core index 1.48, across a thin air gap. Find (a) the total power emitted, (b) the power coupled into the fiber before Fresnel loss, (c) the coupling efficiency in dB, and (d) the power left after Fresnel reflection at the fiber face.
steps: Radii in cm, to match B<sub>0</sub>: r<sub>s</sub> = 35 µm = 3.5×10⁻³ cm; a = 25 µm = 2.5×10⁻³ cm.
Fresnel at the fiber face: R = ((1.48 − 1)/(1.48 + 1))² = (0.48/2.48)² = 0.0375; the face passes 0.9625 (a 0.17 dB loss).
Power in the fiber: 0.247 mW × 0.9625 = 0.237 mW.
examples.answer: P<sub>s</sub> = 12.1 mW, the fiber takes 0.247 mW (η = 0.0204, a 16.9 dB coupling loss), and 0.237 mW remains after Fresnel reflection.

traps: Using NA instead of NA² makes the estimate far too large.
Forgetting the area factor (r<sub>c</sub> / r<sub>s</sub>)² ignores the source-to-core size mismatch.
Radiance and radius must use one length unit: B<sub>0</sub> in W cm⁻² sr⁻¹ needs r in cm, so 35 µm is 3.5×10⁻³ cm.
Mixing radius and diameter changes the area factor by a factor of four.
Ignoring Fresnel reflection misses the near 4% loss at an uncoated air-glass face with n ≈ 1.5, where R = ((n − 1)/(n + 1))² ≈ 0.04.

quiz.a: η is the ratio of power entering the fiber's guided mode to power emitted by the source.

quiz.q: Write the coupling estimate for a small Lambertian LED whose area is no larger than the core.
quiz.a: η ≈ NA², where NA is the fiber numerical aperture.

quiz.q: Why does NA appear squared in the small-LED coupling estimate?
quiz.a: A Lambertian source sends a fraction sin²θ of its power into a cone of half-angle θ. The fiber accepts the cone with sin θ<sub>a</sub> = NA, so the captured fraction is sin²θ<sub>a</sub> = NA².

quiz.q: A large uniform LED has r<sub>s</sub> = 100 µm, P<sub>s</sub> = 1.0 mW. The fiber has r<sub>c</sub> = 50 µm and NA = 0.30. Find the coupled power.
For a larger source, NA is doubled and the core radius is halved. What happens to η?
quiz.a: η depends on NA² and r<sub>c</sub>². Doubling NA multiplies η by 4; halving r<sub>c</sub> multiplies it by 1/4. The two changes cancel, so η stays the same.

quiz.q: What does a lens do in source-to-fiber coupling?
quiz.a: It changes the spot size and ray angles so the source image better matches the fiber core and acceptance cone.

quiz.q: A coupling loss is 3 dB and the input power is 200 µW. Find the coupled power.
quiz.a: 3 dB loss halves the power: 200 µW / 2 = 100 µW.

quiz.q: Why is alignment tolerance tighter for a single-mode pigtail than for a 50 µm multimode pigtail?
quiz.a: A single-mode core and mode field are much smaller, so a lateral error of about 1 µm already causes large overlap loss; a 50 µm multimode core tolerates larger shifts.

beyond: Not for the exam. Silicon photonics uses grating couplers to launch light from a chip into a fiber; photonic wire bonding prints polymer waveguides between chips. Mode-field converters bridge laser and fiber spot sizes. Search: grating coupler efficiency, lensed fiber, photonic wire bonding, mode-field diameter.
